memory_text: Before the road reached our village, Dashain brought every branch of the family home on foot. We swept the stone courtyard, made a bamboo swing, and waited for the eldest hands to place tika and jamara on our foreheads. No one ate alone; even travellers were called in for rice, goat curry, and blessings.
summary: Aama Maya remembers Dashain as a homecoming of shared food, bamboo swings, tika, jamara, and blessings.

memory_text: At Tihar we shaped small oil lamps from clay and placed them along every window ledge. After dark, children walked from house to house singing deusi and bhailo. Each doorway answered with sel roti, fruit, and a little money, and the songs tied the whole settlement together.
summary: Tihar lit the village with clay lamps while deusi-bhailo songs and shared sel roti connected every household.

memory_text: After the mustard and radish leaves were washed, we wilted them in the sun, crushed them firmly, and packed them into an earthen pot. The sealed pot stayed warm for several days before the leaves were spread on a clean mat to dry. That gundruk carried the taste of our winter garden into the monsoon.
summary: Sita Aama preserves winter greens as gundruk through wilting, fermentation in an earthen pot, and sun-drying.

memory_text: Our terraces were repaired before the first monsoon rain. Neighbours exchanged labour instead of money: one day everyone worked our slope, the next day we worked theirs. We planted millet along the edges because its roots held the soil when the rain ran hard.
summary: Tek Bahadur recalls communal labour repairing terraces and millet roots protecting soil before monsoon.

memory_text: The old stone hiti was more than a water spout. Before sunrise we queued with copper vessels, exchanged news, arranged help for sick neighbours, and learned which fields needed hands. When the new pipes came, water moved closer to home, but our morning meeting place grew quiet.
summary: Pabitra Aama remembers the stone hiti as both a water source and the village's morning meeting place.

memory_text: We learned beneath a pipal tree before the school had walls. Children traced letters on wooden boards dusted with soft ash, then wiped them clean for the next lesson. Older pupils helped the younger ones, and every book was wrapped carefully because several children shared it.
summary: Hariprasad recalls shared books, ash-covered writing boards, and peer learning beneath a pipal tree.

memory_text: My grandmother greeted children with the Nepal Bhasa phrase 'Jwojalapa' and taught us that a greeting should slow you down long enough to truly see the person. We used it with elders, neighbours, and guests as a sign of respect and welcome.
summary: Nani Maya explains Jwojalapa as a Nepal Bhasa greeting that carries attention, respect, and welcome.

memory_text: Clay for our pots was tested between finger and thumb before it touched the wheel. My father taught me to centre it by listening to the rhythm of the spinning stone, not by forcing it. Finished vessels dried slowly in shade, then families fired them together in a straw-covered kiln.
summary: Kaji Man remembers learning to centre local clay by rhythm and firing vessels together in a shared kiln.
